engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Thinking Process
chess.body: Every move: 1. What did my opponent just do? (threats?) 2. What are my candidate moves? (at least 2-3) 3. Calculate each candidate 2-3 moves deep. 4. Use LPDO check. 5. Make the move. Don't play on impulse. Even 30 seconds of structured thinking eliminates 80% of blunders. This process is the difference between 800 and 1200 Elo.

wisdom.title: Joy is a Practise
wisdom.body: Joy doesn't arrive when the conditions are right. It's practiced in the conditions you have. Find one thing today that is genuinely good. Savour it for 30 seconds. This is not toxic positivity — it's neurological training. Brains that practise noticing goodness get better at finding it, even in hard seasons.

book.author: Gary Keller
book.chapter: What's the ONE Thing That Makes Everything Else Easier?
book.lesson: Keller's focusing question: 'What is the ONE Thing I can do, such that by doing it, everything else becomes easier or unnecessary?' This question forces prioritisation at the deepest level. Most to-do lists are lists of tasks with no hierarchy. The focusing question demands you find the task that is the linchpin — the one that, if done, makes other tasks unnecessary or simpler. Applied to a business: the one customer that unlocks others. Applied to a career: the one skill that opens all doors. Applied to a day: the one call that makes the rest of the day productive.
book.key_quote: Extraordinary results are directly determined by how narrow you can make your focus.
book.action: Every morning, before opening email, answer: 'What is the ONE Thing I can do today that would make everything else easier?' Do that first.
crux: The focusing question: what's the ONE thing I can do, such that by doing it everything else gets easier or unnecessary?
Success is sequential, not simultaneous. One domino at a time.
A 2-inch domino can topple one 50% larger. Twenty-three dominoes in sequence reach the moon.
Multitasking is a lie. The brain task-switches, and each switch costs time and accuracy.
Willpower is a battery, not a trait. Spend it on the ONE thing, early.
A balanced life is a myth. Counterbalance instead: go extreme on priorities, then return.
Big is not bad. Thinking small caps the outcome before you start.
Time-block the ONE thing first — four hours, daily, protected before anything else enters the calendar.
Protect the block like a surgeon protects theatre time. Interruption is not negotiable.
Goal-set to the now: someday → 5-year → 1-year → month → week → today.
Productivity is not doing more things. It is doing the right thing until it compounds.
Four thieves: inability to say no, fear of chaos, poor health habits, an environment that doesn't support the goal.
learnings: Priorities plural is a contradiction. The word had no plural for 500 years.
Extraordinary results come from narrow, sustained focus — not from breadth.
If everything is important, nothing gets finished.
Chaos elsewhere is the price of excellence somewhere. Accept it consciously.
examples: Gary Keller rebuilt Keller Williams by replacing 14 executives and focusing on one thing at a time; it became the largest real-estate firm in the US.
Pat Matthews sold one painting after a year, then committed to one painting per day. Within two years he was selling at $10,000 each.
The Colonel spent years on one recipe and one method before franchising anything.
adapt: Weekly: name the ONE thing that makes the Dubai offer likelier. Usually it is one specific application done properly, not ten sent.
Time-block 6–8am for it. Everything else takes what remains.
On TradeFlow: ship the measured equity engine well before adding a fifth page.
Counterbalance, don't balance. Job-hunt sprints will cost evenings. Say so out loud and repay the time after.

interview_tech.q: What is EBITDAR and why does retail use it?
interview_tech.a: EBITDA before rent. Retail and hospitality use it because the owned-versus-leased decision distorts EBITDA comparability — a company that owns its stores shows higher EBITDA than an identical company that leases them, purely from capital structure. EBITDAR strips that out. Post-IFRS 16 it matters less for reported figures since operating leases already sit below EBITDA, but it remains standard in valuation and in comparing operators across own-versus-lease models.

interview_tech.q: UAE corporate tax is 9%. How does that change your group structure thinking?
interview_tech.a: It ends the era of treating the UAE as a zero-tax base. Key points: 9% applies above AED 375K taxable income; qualifying free zone persons can still get 0% on qualifying income but the conditions are strict and substance-tested; transfer pricing documentation is now mandatory and OECD-aligned. Practically: intercompany charges between a UAE HQ and operating markets need defensible benchmarking, and management fee structures designed purely for tax will be challenged. Model the effective rate, not the headline rate.

interview_soft.q: How do you give feedback to someone more senior than you?
interview_soft.a: Ask permission, be specific, and stay on observable behaviour and its effect. 'Can I give you a reaction to how the numbers landed in that meeting? When the forecast changed without the bridge, the room stopped trusting the rest of the pack.' No adjectives about them, one concrete instance, and a suggestion. Then stop talking. Most people either avoid this entirely or overcorrect into confrontation.

interview_soft.q: How do you influence people who do not report to you?
interview_soft.a: Retail finance is almost entirely this — Buying, Operations and Retail Heads do not report to you. The answer is currency: work out what each function is measured on and frame your ask in their terms. A buyer cares about sell-through and margin, not about your working capital target — so bring them the SKU-level analysis showing which lines tie up cash without turning. Give people the analysis they cannot build themselves, and influence follows. Name a specific instance and the outcome.

cfo_field.q: Explain a variance in one sentence or you do not understand it yet.
cfo_field.a: 'Margin is down 180bps: 120 from promotional depth in electronics, 40 from freight, 20 mix.' That is a CFO answer. A table of forty lines is a controller answer. The discipline is to decompose until the drivers are additive and then name the largest two. If you cannot make the bridge add up, you have a data problem, not a communication problem.

cfo_field.q: Working capital is where a retail CFO is actually judged.
cfo_field.a: EBITDA gets the headline; the cash conversion cycle gets the board's attention. DIO + DSO − DPO. Retail is inventory-heavy and often near-zero DSO, so the fight is DIO against DPO. Cutting DIO from 95 to 80 days on AED 400M COGS releases roughly AED 16.4M of cash — permanently, without selling a single extra unit. That is a bigger number than most cost programmes deliver, and it does not need a headcount conversation.

Drop all off‑beat lines and master the mainline French Defense (1.e4 e6) and the London System (1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bf4), drilling each move until you can play them without thinking.
